events.title: The Syracusans accuse Marcellus before the Senate
events.summary: Syracusan envoys complained to the Senate about the sack of their city. Marcellus answered them in person and withdrew; the Senate upheld his acts but promised to look after Syracuse. The Syracusans then threw themselves at his feet and took him as their patron, a role his descendants held into Cicero's day.

events.title: Senators give their gold and silver to the state
events.summary: With the treasury empty and the people refusing a new levy of rowers, the consul Laevinus proposed that senators lead by handing over their gold, silver and bronze, keeping only rings, a bulla for each son, a salt cellar and a dish for the gods. Equestrians and plebeians followed, and the contributions were entered in public accounts for repayment.
events.detail: Livy's scene is famous as the archetype of patriotic sacrifice, but the loans were real debts: in 204 the Senate began repaying them in three instalments, and in 200, with the treasury short, the creditors were offered public land within 50 miles of Rome as security (the trientabula). The episode illustrates how the Republic financed total war through its propertied class.

events.title: Roman embassy to Ptolemy IV
events.summary: With Italian agriculture ruined and grain prices extreme, Rome sent an embassy to Alexandria to renew friendship with Ptolemy IV and Arsinoe, bringing a toga, purple tunic and ivory chair for the king and an embroidered robe for the queen, and appealed for grain.

events.title: Philip V besieges Echinus
events.summary: Philip besieged the Aetolian-held town of Echinus on the Malian Gulf with siege towers and mines. Publius Sulpicius Galba with the Roman fleet and the Aetolian general Dorimachus tried to relieve it but were beaten off, and the town surrendered.

sides.strength: garrison, with Roman and Aetolian relief

battle.significance: Showed the limits of the Roman-Aetolian alliance against Philip on land.

events.title: Arson in the Forum
events.summary: On the eve of the Quinquatrus in March 210 fires broke out at several points around the Forum, destroying the Lautumiae, the fish market, the Atrium Regium and the old shops; the temple of Vesta was saved with difficulty. A slave named Manus denounced the Calavii, young Campanian nobles avenging their city, and was freed with 20,000 asses.

events.title: Battle of Canusium
events.summary: Marcellus caught up with Hannibal near Canusium. On the first day the Romans were worsted; Marcellus berated his men, and on the second day, with the disgraced cohorts in front, they drove Hannibal back with elephants turned by javelins and fire. Livy claims 8,000 Carthaginians and 3,000 Romans killed; Marcellus' army was so mauled it spent the summer in Venusia.

sides.losses: c. 2,700 on day one, c. 3,000 on day two (Livy)

battle.significance: Pinned Hannibal while Fabius recovered Tarentum.

events.debate: Livy presents a Roman victory; Plutarch admits Marcellus' heavy losses. Most moderns see a costly draw.

events.title: Gaius Valerius Flaccus forced to become flamen Dialis
events.summary: The pontifex maximus Publius Licinius Crassus compelled the dissolute young Gaius Valerius Flaccus to be inaugurated as priest of Jupiter. The office reformed him, and he then claimed the old right of the flamen Dialis to a seat in the Senate, which had lapsed; the tribunes upheld his claim.

events.title: Philip V defeats the Aetolians near Lamia
events.summary: Philip V twice defeated the Aetolians under Pyrrhias, supported by 1,000 Romans and Pergamene troops sent by Attalus, near Lamia, driving them into the town with heavy losses. Peace talks mediated by Ptolemy IV, Rhodes, Chios and Athens followed but failed.

battle.significance: Kept the Aetolians on the defensive.

events.title: Galba and Attalus take Oreus; Philip surprises Attalus at Opus
events.summary: The Roman fleet under Galba and Attalus I took Oreus in Euboea through the treachery of its commander. When Attalus then sacked Opus in Locris, Philip arrived by forced marches and nearly caught him; Attalus escaped to his ships and soon went home to face Prusias of Bithynia.

events.title: Triumph of Livius Salinator; Nero rides behind
events.summary: For the Metaurus, Marcus Livius Salinator triumphed in a chariot because the battle had been fought in his province, while his colleague Claudius Nero, whose march had won it, followed on horseback without his soldiers. Livy says the crowd's applause went to Nero.

events.title: Battle of Mantinea
events.summary: Philopoemen, general of the Achaean League, whose army he had re-equipped in Macedonian style, defeated the Spartan tyrant Machanidas outside Mantinea, killing him with his own hand at a ditch; some 4,000 Spartans fell. Polybius, Philopoemen's admirer, describes the battle in detail.

sides.strength: Spartan army and mercenaries under Machanidas

battle.significance: Made the Achaean League an independent military power; Machanidas was succeeded by Nabis.

events.title: Silanus defeats Hanno and Mago in Celtiberia
events.summary: Scipio's lieutenant Marcus Junius Silanus surprised the new Carthaginian general Hanno and Mago Barca while they were recruiting in Celtiberia. The 9,000 Celtiberian recruits were scattered; Hanno was captured, while Mago escaped with the cavalry to Gades.

battle.significance: Prevented Carthage from rebuilding its Spanish army with Celtiberian levies.

events.title: Lucius Scipio takes Orongis
events.summary: Scipio's brother Lucius stormed Orongis, a rich town in the mining district of the Maesesses, where Hasdrubal son of Gisco had based himself. Only about 90 Romans fell; Scipio praised the capture as equal to New Carthage.

events.title: Destruction of Iliturgi
events.summary: Iliturgi had betrayed Roman refugees after the defeat of the Scipios in 211. In 206 Scipio stormed it; the soldiers, Livy says, killed everyone including women and infants, and burned the town. Castulo then surrendered without a fight.

battle.significance: Exemplary punishment for the betrayal of 211.

events.title: Mass suicide at Astapa
events.summary: When Lucius Marcius besieged the pro-Carthaginian town of Astapa, its men piled their women, children and valuables in the forum, set guards to burn them, and sallied to die fighting. The guards fired the pyre and threw themselves in; the Romans found only ashes.

battle.significance: One of the most notorious episodes of the Spanish war.

events.title: Funeral games for the Scipios at New Carthage
events.summary: Scipio held games at New Carthage for his father and uncle. The gladiators were volunteers, not slaves, and included two Spanish cousins, Corbis and Orsua, who settled a dispute over a chieftainship by single combat; Corbis won.

events.title: Scipio and Hasdrubal dine with Syphax
events.summary: Scipio crossed to Africa with two quinqueremes to win Syphax, arriving at Siga at the same moment as Hasdrubal son of Gisco, who had escaped from Spain. Syphax entertained both on the same couch; Hasdrubal, Livy says, judged Scipio more formidable in conversation than in battle.

events.title: Masinissa goes over to Rome
events.summary: After Ilipa, the Massylian prince Masinissa, who had fought for Carthage in Spain since 212, met Silanus and then Scipio secretly and pledged himself to Rome. Losing his father's kingdom to Syphax soon afterwards, he spent 205 as a fugitive in the mountains until Scipio landed in Africa.
events.detail: Livy's portrait of their meeting at an unspecified place in Spain (Masinissa 'was struck by the majesty of Scipio') belongs to the Scipionic legend, but the defection itself is certain. Its significance only became clear later: Syphax, after flirting with Rome, married Hasdrubal's daughter Sophonisba and went over to Carthage, so Masinissa's cavalry became the decisive arm of Scipio's African campaign, and his kingdom the instrument of Roman policy in Africa for 50 years.

events.title: The fire of Vesta goes out
events.summary: The sacred fire in the temple of Vesta went out through the negligence of the Vestal on watch. The pontifex maximus had her scourged and the Senate ordered expiation with full-grown victims and a supplication at the temple.

events.title: First Cretan War
events.summary: Encouraged by Philip V's agent Dicaearchus, Cretan cities, especially Hierapytna, waged a pirate war on Rhodes and the Cyclades. Rhodes and its allies eventually defeated them, but the war absorbed Rhodian strength just as Philip expanded in the Aegean.

events.title: Hannibal's inscription at the temple of Juno Lacinia
events.summary: Before leaving Italy, Hannibal set up a bronze tablet in Punic and Greek at the temple of Hera (Juno) Lacinia recording his deeds and the strength of his army. Polybius read it and used its figures, for example the 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse with which Hannibal reached Italy.
events.debate: Livy puts the dedication in 205; it may date to Hannibal's last summer in Bruttium in 205 or 204.

events.title: Final defeat and death of Indibilis
events.summary: Scipio's departure encouraged Indibilis of the Ilergetes and Mandonius to rise again. The proconsuls Lucius Lentulus and Lucius Manlius Acidinus crushed their army; Indibilis was killed and the Spaniards surrendered Mandonius and other leaders for execution.

battle.significance: Ended the Ilergetan revolts; northern Spain stayed under Roman control.

events.title: The Etruscan and Umbrian contributions to Scipio's fleet
events.summary: Denied a levy by a reluctant Senate, Scipio raised volunteers and accepted gifts from allies: Caere grain, Populonia iron, Tarquinii sailcloth, Volaterrae ship fittings and grain, Arretium 3,000 shields, 3,000 helmets, 50,000 javelins and pikes, Perusia, Clusium and Rusellae fir timber. Thirty ships were built 45 days after the timber was cut.
events.detail: Livy's list is a precious snapshot of the economic geography of central Italy: Populonia smelting Elban iron, Arretium's arms industry, Tarquinii's linen, and timber from the Apennine and Etruscan forests. It also shows the political struggle: Fabius Maximus argued in the Senate that Scipio should stay in Italy until Hannibal was gone, and the Senate gave Scipio Sicily with permission to cross to Africa 'if it was in the interest of the state', but only the Cannae legions as an army.
scholarship: Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971)

events.title: Temple of Honos and Virtus dedicated
events.summary: Marcus Marcellus, son of the hero, dedicated the double temple of Honos and Virtus at the Porta Capena, vowed by his father at Clastidium (222). The pontiffs had ruled that one cella could not house two gods, so Virtus received her own shrine; the temple became a museum of Syracusan art.

events.title: The great revolt of the Thebaid
events.summary: In the last years of Ptolemy IV native Egyptian pharaohs, Haronnophris and then Chaonnophris, ruled the Thebaid from Thebes for some twenty years with priestly support. Ptolemaic forces regained the south only in 186, when Chaonnophris was defeated near Syene.
events.detail: Papyri and dated documents show the rebel pharaohs' regnal years at Thebes from 205. The revolt, rooted in the arming of native Egyptians for Raphia (217) and in fiscal pressure, cut Alexandria off from the grain and gold of the south and weakened Egypt just as Antiochus III and Philip V moved against its overseas possessions. The Rosetta decree of 196 mentions the siege of Lycopolis in the Delta, a separate rebel centre.

events.title: Cavalry battle near Salaeca
events.summary: Soon after landing, Scipio used Masinissa, who feigned retreat with a small force, to draw the Carthaginian cavalry under Hanno son of Hamilcar into an ambush near the tower of Salaeca. Hanno was killed with about 1,000 of his men and some 2,000 were captured.

battle.significance: Gave Scipio freedom to ravage the Carthaginian countryside.

events.title: Battle near Croton
events.summary: The consul Publius Sempronius Tuditanus fought Hannibal near Croton; Livy reports a defeat with 1,200 Roman dead and then a victory the next day with the help of the proconsul Licinius Crassus, killing 4,000. One of the last pitched actions of Hannibal in Italy.

battle.significance: Kept Hannibal confined to Bruttium.

events.title: Naval battle off Utica
events.summary: While Scipio was at Tunis after the Great Plains, the Carthaginian fleet sailed against his warships beached before Utica. Scipio lashed his transports four deep into a floating wall to protect them; the Carthaginians, attacking with grapnels, towed off about 60 transports but failed to destroy the fleet.

sides.strength: warships behind a line of transports

battle.significance: Carthage's last notable naval effort of the war.

events.title: Fall of Agathocles in Alexandria
events.summary: Agathocles, who with Sosibius had concealed Ptolemy IV's death and had Queen Arsinoe III murdered to rule for the child Ptolemy V, was overthrown when the Macedonian guard and the Alexandrian crowd rose under Tlepolemus. Agathocles, his sister Agathoclea and their mother were torn to pieces in the stadium.
events.detail: Polybius' long, vivid account of the lynching (15.25-33), complete with a criticism of historians who sensationalise such scenes, is a key source for Alexandrian politics. Egypt's paralysis under a child king and rival regents invited the 'pact of the kings' and Antiochus' invasion of Coele-Syria, and prompted the appeals that drew Rome east in 200.

events.title: Battle of Lade
events.summary: In the same campaign as Chios, Philip V defeated the Rhodian fleet off the island of Lade near Miletus. The Milesians crowned Philip and his admiral Heraclides, and Philip went on to plunder Caria, where in winter 201/200 the Rhodian and Pergamene fleets blockaded him in Bargylia.

battle.significance: Encouraged Rhodes and Pergamon to appeal to Rome.

events.debate: The relative order of Lade and Chios is disputed; Polybius criticises the Rhodian historians Zeno and Antisthenes for claiming Lade as a Rhodian success.

events.title: Antiochus III takes Gaza
events.summary: Opening the Fifth Syrian War, Antiochus III besieged and took Gaza, whose loyalty to the Ptolemies Polybius praises. The fall of Gaza opened the road to Egypt and prompted the Ptolemaic counter-offensive under Scopas.

battle.significance: Opened the Fifth Syrian War.

events.title: Plautus' Stichus at the Plebeian Games
events.summary: The surviving production notice (didascalia) of Plautus' Stichus dates its staging to the Ludi Plebeii of 200, with music by Marcipor, slave of Oppius, and adapted from Menander's Adelphoi. It is one of only two Plautine plays with a secure date; the other is the Pseudolus of 191.

events.title: Fabius Pictor writes the first Roman history
events.summary: Around 200 the senator Quintus Fabius Pictor, a veteran of the Gallic war of 225 and envoy to Delphi after Cannae, wrote a history of Rome in Greek from Aeneas and Romulus to his own day, aimed largely at Greek readers. It was the foundation of the Roman annalistic tradition.
events.detail: Polybius used Fabius alongside the pro-Carthaginian Philinus for the First Punic War and accuses him of bias, especially in blaming the Second War on Hasdrubal's ambition and the Barcid faction rather than Carthage as a whole. Fabius dated the foundation of Rome to the first year of the eighth Olympiad (748/7). Writing in Greek gave the Roman case a hearing in the Hellenistic world at the moment Rome entered it; Cato's Latin Origines a generation later was partly a reaction. A painted inscription from a library at Tauromenium preserves a summary of Fabius' work.
scholarship: Badian, The Early Historians, in Dorey (ed.), Latin Historians (1966)
Dillery, Quintus Fabius Pictor and Greco-Roman Historiography at Rome, in Vertis in Usum (2002)

events.title: Battle of Ottolobus
events.summary: Publius Sulpicius Galba, invading Macedonia from Illyria, won a cavalry and light infantry action near Ottolobus in Lyncestis; Philip V was nearly caught when his horse was killed and survived only because a guardsman gave him his own. Galba then took Pelium and retired to Apollonia.

battle.significance: First Roman success of the war, but without strategic result.

events.title: Claudius Centho raids Chalcis
events.summary: A Roman squadron under Gaius Claudius Centho, sent to help Athens, surprised Chalcis at dawn, burned the Macedonian arsenal and granaries, freed prisoners held there and destroyed the royal statues before withdrawing. Philip, arriving too late, marched on Athens in revenge.

events.title: Philip V at the gates of Athens
events.summary: Philip attacked Athens at dawn and fought a cavalry battle at the Dipylon, then, unable to take the city, ravaged Attica, destroying the Academy, the Lyceum, shrines and tombs. Athens answered by abolishing the honours of the Antigonids and cursing Philip and his ancestors.

battle.significance: Turned Greek opinion against Philip.

events.title: Ovation of Lucius Cornelius Lentulus
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, who had held command in Spain without holding a magistracy (as a privatus cum imperio), asked for a triumph. The Senate replied that no one had triumphed who had not held office as dictator, consul or praetor and allowed only an ovation; a tribune's veto was overcome.
events.detail: The decision set the rule applied again to Lucius Manlius Acidinus in 199 and to the Spanish commanders of the 190s, and was cited in the debates over Pompey in 81 and 71. It shows the Senate regulating the honours of the prorogued and extraordinary commands that the Second Punic War had multiplied. Lentulus brought 44,000 pounds of silver and 2,450 of gold from Spain.

events.title: Public land in lieu of repayment: the trientabula
events.summary: The creditors who had lent to the state in 210 were due their third instalment in 200, but the treasury needed money for the Macedonian war. The Senate offered them public land within 50 miles of Rome at a nominal rent of one as per iugerum, redeemable for cash later; the land was called trientabulum because it stood for a third of the debt.

events.title: Scopas surrenders at Sidon
events.summary: After Panium, Scopas shut himself up in Sidon with 10,000 men. Blockaded by Antiochus III and starving, he surrendered and was allowed to leave without arms; Antiochus then took the rest of Phoenicia, Judaea, where Jerusalem welcomed him, and Coele-Syria.

battle.significance: Completed the Seleucid conquest of Coele-Syria.

events.title: Siege of Atrax
events.summary: Flamininus breached the walls of Atrax, but the Macedonian garrison formed a phalanx in the breach and the legionaries could not shift it; a siege tower stuck in the rubble. Flamininus abandoned the siege, an episode Livy uses to show the phalanx's strength on a narrow front.

battle.significance: Rare example of the phalanx beating legionaries in the breach.

events.title: Capture of Eretria
events.summary: The combined fleets of Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, Attalus I and Rhodes besieged Eretria; the Macedonian garrison surrendered the citadel. Livy notes that few gold and silver objects but many statues, paintings and old works of art were taken, an early sign of Rome's appetite for Greek art.

events.title: Flamininus takes Elatea
events.summary: After the Aous, Flamininus overran Phocis and stormed Elatea, which he then used as his winter base, while his diplomats won over the Achaean League at Sicyon.

events.title: Death of Attalus I
events.summary: Attalus I, aged 72, collapsed with a stroke while addressing the Boeotian assembly at Thebes in spring 197 in support of Rome, and was carried home to Pergamon to die. He had founded the dynasty's royal title by defeating the Galatians and had made Pergamon Rome's indispensable eastern ally. His son Eumenes II succeeded.
events.detail: Polybius' obituary (18.41) praises Attalus as a king who won his throne by merit, lived 72 years and reigned 44, and left four grown sons in perfect harmony. His victory over the Galatians (c. 238) was commemorated by the dedication of statues of dying Gauls on the Pergamene acropolis, of which the Dying Gaul and Ludovisi Gaul in Rome are copies; the Lesser Attalid dedication on the Athenian acropolis followed. He had brought the Magna Mater's stone to Rome in 205 and fought beside Rome in both Macedonian wars.

events.title: Battle of Turda
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Minucius Thermus defeated the Spanish chiefs Budares and Baesadines near the town of Turda, claiming 12,000 enemy dead and the capture of Budares, part of the suppression of the great Spanish revolt of 197.

events.title: Marcellus defeats the Insubres and takes Comum
events.summary: The consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus, after a reverse at the hands of the Boii, crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres and the people of Comum, taking 28 strongholds, and triumphed. His colleague Furius Purpurio worked with him in the Boian country.

battle.significance: Broke Insubrian resistance north of the Po.

events.title: The Memphis decree (Rosetta Stone)
events.summary: On 27 March 196 a synod of Egyptian priests at Memphis decreed honours for Ptolemy V on the first anniversary of his coronation, in thanks for tax remissions, temple gifts and the suppression of rebels at Lycopolis. Copies were set up in temples in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek; one, found at Rashid in 1799, made possible Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs.
events.detail: The decree illustrates the bargain between the Ptolemaic crown and the native priesthood at a moment of weakness: the king had lost Coele-Syria to Antiochus III, the Thebaid was in revolt, and he needed the temples' support. In return for confirming priestly revenues, remitting arrears and taking part in Egyptian rites of coronation at Memphis, Ptolemy was to be honoured as a god with statues in every temple. The stone (British Museum EA 24) is a granodiorite stela, broken at the top; other copies of the decree are known from Nubayrah and Elephantine.
scholarship: Parkinson, Cracking Codes: The Rosetta Stone and Decipherment (1999)

events.title: Valerius Flaccus defeats the Boii near the Litana forest
events.summary: The consul Lucius Valerius Flaccus, Cato's colleague, defeated the Boii near the Litana forest where Postumius' army had been destroyed in 216, reportedly killing 8,000, and spent the rest of the year rebuilding Placentia and Cremona.

events.title: Cato disarms Hispania Citerior
events.summary: After Emporiae, Cato sent sealed letters to the communities north of the Ebro ordering them to demolish their walls on the same day; most complied for fear that each was the only one ordered. He also organised the silver and iron mines for revenue, and boasted that he had taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain.
events.detail: Livy says Cato's revenues from the mines, especially around New Carthage and in the north, made the province profitable (34.21). Plutarch claims Cato took 400 towns; Cato's own speeches survive in fragments and made the most of his campaign. The Celtiberian mercenaries whom the Turdetani hired against him he tried to buy off with double pay. Cato's settlement did not last: the Spanish wars resumed within two years, but his organisation of tribute and mining set patterns for the next generation.

events.title: The sacred spring fulfilled
events.summary: The ver sacrum vowed in 217 after Trasimene, the dedication to Jupiter of all livestock born in one spring, was finally performed in 195. The pontifex maximus Licinius Crassus declared it improperly done, and it was repeated in 194, covering animals born between 1 March and 30 April.

events.title: Senators given separate seats at the games
events.summary: At the Ludi Romani of 194, on the order of the censors Sextus Aelius Paetus and Gaius Cornelius Cethegus (supported, it was said, by Scipio Africanus in his second consulship), the curule aediles reserved separate seats for senators. Livy reports popular resentment and Africanus' later regret.

events.title: Temples of Juno Sospita, Faunus and Fortuna Primigenia dedicated
events.summary: In 194 Gaius Cornelius Cethegus dedicated the temple of Juno Sospita in the vegetable market, vowed at the Mincius; plebeian aediles dedicated a temple of Faunus on the Tiber island from fines on graziers; and a temple of Fortuna Primigenia, vowed by Sempronius Tuditanus in 204 and modelled on the cult of Praeneste, was dedicated on the Quirinal.
events.locName: Forum Holitorium, Tiber Island and Quirinal, Rome

events.title: Triumph of Cato over Spain
events.summary: Cato triumphed over Hispania Citerior, displaying 25,000 pounds of silver bullion, 123,000 bigati, 540 pounds of Oscan silver and 1,400 pounds of gold, and gave each soldier 270 asses. He then served as a legate under others, refusing to rest on his triumph.

events.title: Scipio Nasica defeats the Lusitanians near Ilipa
events.summary: The praetor Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica intercepted a Lusitanian raiding army returning laden with booty from Ulterior near Ilipa and defeated it, claiming 12,000 killed and recovering the plunder.

events.title: Marriage of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I
events.summary: In the winter of 194/3, sealing the peace that ended the Fifth Syrian War, Antiochus III married his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy V at Raphia. Ptolemaic courtiers later claimed the dowry included the revenues or even the possession of Coele-Syria, a claim that fuelled the Sixth Syrian War.

events.title: Ligurians besiege Pisae
events.summary: A Ligurian army of 40,000, Livy says, ravaged the territory of Luna and besieged Pisae. The consul Quintus Minucius Thermus held the city in 193 and in 192 defeated the Ligurians near Pisae, killing 9,000, the start of four years of command against them.

events.title: Fulvius Nobilior at Toletum
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Fulvius Nobilior defeated a coalition of Vaccaei, Vettones and Celtiberians near Toletum and captured their king Hilermus; in 192 he stormed Toletum itself, the first Roman advance onto the Meseta.

battle.significance: First Roman push into the central Meseta.

events.title: The conversation of Hannibal and Scipio at Ephesus
events.summary: When Roman envoys, among them Publius Villius Tappulus and perhaps Scipio Africanus, came to Antiochus' court in 193, the Romans conferred with Hannibal. Tradition reported that Scipio asked who was the greatest general: Hannibal answered Alexander, then Pyrrhus, then himself, and added that had he beaten Scipio he would have put himself first.
events.debate: Livy found the story in Claudius Quadrigarius, who followed Acilius' Greek history; many regard the meeting as a literary invention, though Villius' embassy and the Romans' talks with Hannibal, which made Antiochus distrust him, are accepted.

events.title: Tiber floods and the fire of 192
events.summary: In 193 the Tiber flooded twice, destroying two bridges and many buildings around the Porta Flumentana; a landslide fell from the Capitol onto the Vicus Iugarius. In 192 a fire burned the buildings along the Tiber for two days, and there were twelve floods in the year.

events.title: Temple of Veiovis on the Capitol
events.summary: Quintus Marcius Ralla dedicated a temple of Veiovis between the two summits of the Capitol, vowed by Lucius Furius Purpurio in his Gallic battle of 200. Its later rebuilding survives beneath the Tabularium.

events.title: Philopoemen defeats Nabis near Gythium
events.summary: Philopoemen, whose naval attempt to relieve Gythium failed when his old flagship broke up, ambushed Nabis' army in rough country near Mount Barbosthenes, killing many and pursuing the tyrant to Sparta. The Romans, preoccupied with Antiochus, imposed a truce.

battle.significance: Weakened Nabis shortly before his murder by the Aetolians.

events.title: Antiochus III winters at Chalcis and marries
events.summary: Antiochus, aged about fifty, spent the winter of 192/1 at Chalcis, where he married a young Chalcidian, daughter of Cleoptolemus, whom he named Euboea. Polybius and Livy made the wedding festivities the symbol of the king's lost momentum before Thermopylae.

events.title: Lex Acilia on intercalation
events.summary: Macrobius, citing Varro, says that the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio carried a law in 191 giving the pontiffs discretion over intercalation. The Roman calendar was then badly out of step with the seasons, as the eclipse reported by Livy for 190 shows.
events.debate: The interpretation is debated: whether the law granted discretion (and so allowed abuse) or tried to restore regular intercalation after wartime neglect.

events.title: Plautus' Pseudolus at the dedication of the Magna Mater temple
events.summary: The didascalia of the Pseudolus records its production at the Ludi Megalenses of 191, the games celebrating the dedication of the Magna Mater's temple on the Palatine, with the urban praetor Marcus Junius Brutus presiding. The play, about a scheming slave, was performed on a temporary stage in front of the temple.

events.title: Temple of Juventas dedicated
events.summary: Gaius Licinius Lucullus dedicated a temple of Juventas (Youth) at the Circus Maximus, vowed by Marcus Livius Salinator on the day of the Metaurus sixteen years earlier.

events.title: Siege of Naupactus
events.summary: After Heraclea, Acilius Glabrio besieged the Aetolians in Naupactus for two months. Flamininus, worried that the Achaeans and Philip were gaining at Aetolian expense, walked up to the walls, was recognised and arranged a truce to let the Aetolians send envoys to Rome.

events.title: Carthage offers to pay its indemnity at once
events.summary: Ten years after Zama, Carthaginian envoys offered to pay the remaining 40 annual instalments of the war indemnity immediately, and to supply grain and a fleet for the war against Antiochus. Rome took the grain but refused the lump sum, preferring the annual tribute as a mark of Carthage's subjection.
events.detail: The offer shows how quickly Carthage recovered economically after 201, aided by Hannibal's reforms of state finance in 196. Archaeology of the circular military harbour and new residential quarters on the Byrsa slope belongs to this period of prosperity. Rome's refusal and its tolerance of Masinissa's encroachments reveal that it valued the dependency more than the money, and the prosperity later alarmed Cato.

events.title: The eclipse that dates the Roman calendar
events.summary: Livy reports that during the Ludi Apollinares, on the fifth day before the Ides of Quinctilis (11 July by the Roman calendar) of 190, the sun was darkened as the moon passed in front of it. Astronomical tables identify this as the partial eclipse of 14 March 190 BC (Julian), showing the Roman calendar about four months ahead of the solar year.
events.detail: This and the lunar eclipse before Pydna (Livy's 3/4 September, in fact 21 June 168) are the key anchors for converting Roman dates of the early second century: the calendar drifted far ahead during the Second Punic War, presumably because intercalation was neglected, and was brought back towards the seasons in the 180s and 170s, perhaps under the lex Acilia of 191. Battles such as Magnesia (late 190 or early 189 Julian) and Cynoscephalae have to be dated with this offset in mind.
scholarship: Derow, The Roman Calendar 190-168 BC, Phoenix 27 (1973)

events.title: Polyxenidas destroys the Rhodian squadron at Panormus
events.summary: Polyxenidas, himself a Rhodian exile, lured the Rhodian admiral Pausistratus with a pretended offer to betray the Seleucid fleet, then caught his 36 ships at Panormus. Pausistratus died fighting; only seven ships escaped by using fire pots slung on poles.
events.locName: Panormus, on the coast near Ephesus/Samos

battle.significance: The fire-pot device used by the survivors became a Rhodian speciality.

events.title: Siege and sack of Phocaea
events.summary: The praetor Aemilius Regillus besieged Phocaea, which had gone over to Antiochus; after Myonessus it surrendered on terms, but the Roman soldiers sacked it anyway. Regillus restored the town and its laws.

events.title: Aemilius Paullus defeated at Lyco
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the future victor of Pydna, then propraetor in Ulterior, was routed by the Lusitanians near Lyco in Bastetania, losing 6,000 men, and only just held his camp. He recovered and won a large victory in 189.

battle.significance: A rare defeat for Paullus.

events.title: Placentia and Cremona reinforced
events.summary: The two Latin colonies on the Po, depleted by war and Gallic attacks, petitioned for new settlers; the Senate sent 6,000 families to be divided between them. The following year a new colony was founded at Bononia.

events.title: Battle of Mount Magaba
events.summary: Having stormed the Tolistobogii on Mount Olympus, Manlius Vulso marched on the Tectosages and Trocmi gathered on Mount Magaba near Ancyra. Roman missile troops again drove the Galatians from their hill position, and their camp and families were captured. The Galatians sued for peace.

battle.significance: Broke Galatian power in western Anatolia for a generation.

events.title: Siege of Same in Cephallenia
events.summary: After the Aetolian peace, Same in Cephallenia, which had surrendered, rose again fearing deportation. Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged it for four months; slingers from Aegium, Patrae and Dyme helped. When it fell the inhabitants were sold into slavery.

battle.significance: Last act of the Aetolian war.

events.title: Acilius Glabrio withdraws from the censorship race
events.summary: Manius Acilius Glabrio, victor of Thermopylae and a new man, stood for the censorship of 189 with lavish gifts to voters. Two tribunes accused him of keeping royal booty from Antiochus' camp, and Cato, his former legate, testified that vessels he had seen in the camp were missing from the triumph. Glabrio withdrew and the prosecution was dropped.
events.detail: The censors elected instead were Titus Flamininus and Marcus Claudius Marcellus. The episode is the first of the peculatus attacks that culminated in the trials of the Scipios two years later, and shows how the profits of eastern war became a political weapon in the competitive aristocracy. Livy notes the hostility of the nobility to a novus homo aspiring to the censorship.

events.title: Census of 189: 258,318 citizens
events.summary: The censors Titus Flamininus and Marcus Claudius Marcellus registered 258,318 citizens, nearly double the figure of 209 (137,108) and well up on 194 (143,704), and for the first time registered the people of Campanian towns, whose census had been taken at Capua. They chose Scipio Africanus princeps senatus for the third time.
events.debate: The low 194 figure probably reflects underregistration and men overseas rather than real losses (Brunt).

events.title: Triumph of Lucius Scipio Asiaticus
events.summary: On the last day of February 189 Lucius Cornelius Scipio triumphed over Antiochus, displaying 224 military standards, 134 town models, 1,231 ivory tusks, 234 gold crowns, 137,420 pounds of silver, 224,000 Attic tetradrachms and 140,000 gold Philippics, and took the cognomen Asiaticus (Asiagenes in the Fasti).

events.title: Philopoemen razes the walls of Sparta
events.summary: After Spartan exiles attacked Las, Philopoemen marched on Sparta. At Compasion some 80 (Polybius) or 350 (Aristocrates) Spartans were killed or executed; Sparta's walls were pulled down, its mercenaries and Nabis' new citizens expelled or sold, and the laws of Lycurgus abolished in favour of Achaean institutions.
events.detail: Livy calls it the destruction of the 'sinews' of Sparta. The episode embittered relations between Sparta and the Achaeans for forty years: Spartan exiles and factions repeatedly appealed to the Roman Senate, which sent envoys (Caecilius Metellus 185, Appius Claudius 184) and sought to arbitrate without fully committing itself. Polybius, from Philopoemen's own circle, defends the action. The Spartan question was the immediate cause of the Achaean War of 146.

events.title: Thracians ambush Manlius Vulso's army
events.summary: Marching home overland from Asia with the Galatian booty, Manlius Vulso's column was attacked by some 10,000 Thracians of the Asti, Caeni and others in a wooded defile. The baggage train was plundered and Quintus Minucius Thermus was among the dead.

battle.significance: Fuelled the opposition to Vulso's triumph.

events.title: Twelve thousand Latins sent home
events.summary: Envoys of the Latin allies complained that their citizens had migrated to Rome and been registered there, draining their manpower for the allied levies. The praetor Quintus Terentius Culleo traced those registered at Rome since 204 and sent 12,000 back to their communities.
events.detail: The expulsions of 187 and 177 (lex Claudia), and again in 172, reflect the tension between the Latin right of migration (ius migrandi) and the allied obligation to supply troops by a fixed formula. As Italians moved to Rome and to the new colonies, the communities left behind struggled to meet their quotas, and Rome, needing the soldiers, sided with the local elites. The issue foreshadowed the citizenship question of the Gracchan age.
scholarship: Broadhead, Rome's Migration Policy and the So-called Ius Migrandi, CCG 12 (2001)

events.title: Triumph of Fulvius Nobilior and the Muses of Ambracia
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior triumphed over the Aetolians and Cephallenia, carrying 785 bronze and 230 marble statues from Ambracia. He installed the statues of the Nine Muses in a temple of Hercules of the Muses (Hercules Musarum) in the Campus Martius and placed there a calendar with commentary (Fasti). Ennius, who had accompanied him, celebrated the campaign in his Ambracia.
events.detail: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Fulvius' enemy, tried to block the triumph by charging him with plundering Ambracia; Cato attacked him for taking a poet on campaign. The temple of Hercules Musarum, later rebuilt by Marcius Philippus (29 BC), introduced the Greek idea of the museum and of the poet as client of the general. Coins of Q. Pomponius Musa (c. 66) reproduce the Muse statues.

events.title: Lepidus and Flaminius subdue the Friniates and Apuani
events.summary: The consuls of 187, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Gaius Flaminius (son of the consul of 217), campaigned in the Apennines, forcing the Friniates and some Apuani down from their mountain strongholds into the plains. Flaminius built a road from Bononia to Arretium; Lepidus the Via Aemilia.

events.title: The Saltus Marcius disaster
events.summary: The consul Quintus Marcius Philippus pursued the Apuani into a narrow wooded pass where they ambushed him, killing about 4,000 men and taking three standards of the second legion and eleven allied ones. The place, Livy says, was afterwards called the Saltus Marcius.

battle.significance: The worst Roman defeat in the Ligurian wars.

events.title: Deserted colonies of Sipontum and Buxentum resettled
events.summary: The consul Spurius Postumius, travelling through Italy during the Bacchanalia inquiry, found that the citizen colonies of Sipontum and Buxentum, founded in 194, had been deserted by their settlers. New colonists were enrolled in 186 and sent out the following year.

events.title: Transalpine Gauls settle near the site of Aquileia
events.summary: About 12,000 armed Transalpine Gauls crossed into Venetia and began building a town near the future Aquileia without asking permission. After embassies across the Alps, the Romans disarmed them in 183 and sent them back, and the Senate decided to plant a Latin colony there.
events.detail: The Senate's reply to the Gauls, as Livy reports it, was that the Alps were a nearly impassable frontier which Rome intended to defend. Gallic chiefs from beyond the Alps disowned the migrants and Roman envoys went to them. The episode explains the foundation of Aquileia in 181 and is an early instance of Rome treating the Alps as Italy's boundary.

events.title: War of Eumenes II and Prusias I; Hannibal's snake jars
events.summary: Prusias I of Bithynia fought Eumenes II over disputed borderland, with Hannibal as his admiral. Nepos tells how Hannibal had jars filled with snakes thrown onto Pergamene decks to throw the crews into panic. A Roman embassy under Flamininus imposed peace in 183, and Hannibal's surrender was demanded.

battle.significance: Hannibal's last victory.

events.title: Battle of the Tagus
events.summary: After a defeat in 186, the praetors Gaius Calpurnius Piso and Lucius Quinctius Crispinus forced a crossing of the Tagus against Carpetani and Celtiberians and won a large victory, claiming 35,000 enemy dead. Both triumphed in 184.

battle.significance: Secured the Tagus line before the First Celtiberian War.

events.title: Conspiracy of the Apulian herdsmen
events.summary: The praetor Lucius Postumius, sent to Tarentum, investigated a 'great conspiracy of shepherds' who had made the roads and pasturelands unsafe, and condemned about 7,000 men; many escaped. He also continued the Bacchanalian inquiry in the south.
events.detail: The episode is the first notice of trouble from the armed slave herdsmen who drove flocks between the Apulian lowlands and the Samnite mountains on transhumance routes (calles), a system that grew with the ager publicus confiscated after the Hannibalic war. The same population, along with Sicily's estate slaves, supplied recruits for the slave wars of 135 and 73.

events.title: The massacre at Maronea
events.summary: When a Roman commission ordered Philip V to withdraw his garrisons from the Thracian coast, his agent Onomastus and the officer Cassander let Thracians into Maronea at night to massacre the anti-Macedonian citizens. Rome demanded Onomastus and Cassander; Philip sent only Cassander, who died on the way, it was said by poison.
